claims.text: High-entropy-alloy liquids and solids near melting exhibit extensive configurational diversity.
Conventional EAM potentials cannot adequately represent the large variety of atomic configurations in high-temperature HEA liquids.
TOR-TILD uses conventional EAM potentials as reference models.
Actively learned MLIPs will capture the configurational diversity of HEA liquids and solids better than EAM references.
Machine-learned interatomic potentials can map three-dimensional atomic configurations to conformational energies with high accuracy and reduced computational cost.
Structural descriptors in MLIPs represent individual local chemical and structural environments.
Moment tensor potentials using descriptors such as atom-centered symmetry functions are suitable reference models for this thermodynamic-integration intervention.
Active learning continuously enriches the MLIP training set with configurations underrepresented by standard EAM methods.
Enriching the training set with underrepresented configurations improves phase-space overlap between the MLIP reference and the ab initio target.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap produces a more realistic thermodynamic-integration path with less mismatch.
The intervention applies to refractory or high-melting HEAs, especially equimolar solid solutions.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 3000–3600 K.
Both solid and liquid states are relevant in the stated 3000–3600 K range for the targeted HEAs.
Replacing EAM references with actively learned MLIPs will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 30–50%.
MLIP-based thermodynamic integration will converge more closely to ab initio free-energy values than EAM-based TOR-TILD.
The benefit of MLIPs should be less pronounced in elemental or binary systems because EAM potentials already perform adequately there.
The precise reduction in integration-path mismatch is system-dependent.
A controlled comparison of EAM- and MLIP-referenced thermodynamic integration in both solid and liquid phases can test the hypothesis.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction of about 30% or more in path mismatch, together with failure to improve agreement with ab initio free-energy benchmarks, is specified as the rejection criterion.
